title: Mental Health Is Health
bigQuestion: How can we take care of our minds and feelings the way we take care of our bodies?

story.title: The Worry Gets Lighter
story.kicker: Maya carried a worry for weeks. Then she told someone.
paragraphs: Maya was in fourth grade. For three weeks, she had a worry. Her grandma was sick, and Maya thought about it all the time. She thought about it at lunch. She thought about it in bed at night. Her stomach felt tight most mornings.
Maya did not tell anyone. She thought the worry was too small for grown-ups. She also thought it was too big to say out loud. So she kept it inside, and it felt heavier each day.

One morning her teacher, Mr. Ortiz, noticed she was quiet. He asked if she wanted to visit Ms. Bell, the school counselor. Maya said yes. Ms. Bell had a calm room with a soft chair and a bowl of smooth stones.

Maya told Ms. Bell about her grandma. Ms. Bell listened without rushing. She said many kids feel worried when someone they love is sick. She showed Maya a slow breathing trick. They made a plan to talk with Maya's mom that night.
Walking back to class, Maya noticed something. The worry was still there, but it felt lighter. Telling someone had not fixed everything. It had made the worry easier to carry.
story.think: Why do you think the worry felt lighter after Maya talked to Ms. Bell, even though her grandma was still sick?

lessons.title: Feelings Start in the Brain
lessons.mainIdea: Your brain makes feelings, and feelings are signals that help you notice what is going on.
reading: Think about the moment before a spelling test. Your heart may beat fast. Your hands may feel sweaty. That is your body reacting to a feeling. The feeling started in your *brain*.

Your brain is the control center of your body. It sits inside your skull. It helps you think, move and remember. It also makes your *emotions*. Emotions are feelings like happy, sad, scared, angry and excited.

Every feeling is a kind of signal. Fear can tell you to be careful. Sadness can tell you that you miss someone. Happiness can tell you that something is good for you. No feeling is bad to have. What matters is what you do with it.

words.d: the organ inside your head that controls thinking, moving, remembering and feeling
feelings such as happy, sad, angry, scared or excited

look.title: Two Kids, One Feeling
look.text: Jamal is about to read aloud in class. His heart beats fast and his cheeks feel warm. Lena is about to ride a big roller coaster. Her heart beats fast and her cheeks feel warm too.
look.prompt: What feeling might both kids have? How is the same feeling showing up in their bodies?

check.q: Where do feelings start?
check.why: The reading says feelings are made by the brain, the body's control center.

check.q: What is an emotion?
choices: A feeling like happy, sad or scared
check.why: Emotions are feelings such as happy, sad, scared, angry and excited.

check.q: What does the reading say about feelings?
choices: Every feeling is a kind of signal
Kids do not have real feelings
check.why: The reading says every feeling is a signal, and no feeling is bad to have.

lessons.title: Mental Health Is Health
lessons.mainIdea: Mental health is how we think, feel and get along, and it matters as much as body health.
reading: When you scrape your knee, you clean it and put on a bandage. You take care of your body. Your mind needs care too. How you think, feel and get along with others is called *mental health*.
Everyone has mental health, just like everyone has body health. Some days it feels strong. Some days it feels shaky. That is normal. A hard day does not mean something is wrong with you.

Doctors and scientists agree that mind and body are connected. The World Health Organization says health means doing well in body, mind and with other people. Taking care of your feelings is part of taking care of your whole self. This is called *well-being*.

words.d: how well we think, feel, handle stress and get along with others
feeling well in your body, your mind and your life with others

look.title: What Is Health?
look.text: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
look.prompt: The WHO names three parts of health. What are they? Why might it say health is more than not being sick?

check.q: What is mental health?
choices: How you think, feel and get along with others
check.why: Mental health is about thinking, feeling and getting along with others.

check.q: What does a hard day mean, according to the reading?
choices: It is normal and does not mean something is wrong
You are not healthy at all
check.why: The reading says some days feel shaky, and that is normal.

check.q: Which three parts of health does the World Health Organization name?
choices: Body, mind and life with other people
check.why: The WHO describes physical, mental and social well-being.

lessons.title: Naming Your Feelings
lessons.mainIdea: Putting a name on a feeling can help you understand it and calm it.
reading: Picture a boy named Theo. He stomps into the house after soccer. His mom asks what is wrong. At first he says, "Nothing!" Then he stops and says, "I feel embarrassed. I missed the goal."
Theo just did something helpful. He named his feeling. Saying "I feel embarrassed" is clearer than stomping. Now his mom knows how to help. Theo knows too.

Scientists who study the brain have found that putting feelings into words can help calm strong feelings. A list of feeling words is sometimes called a *feelings vocabulary*. The more words you know, the better you can say what is going on inside. Words like frustrated, nervous, proud and lonely are good ones to learn.

words.d: the words you know for naming your feelings
upset because something is hard or is not going the way you want

look.title: Find the Word
look.text: Ana's best friend sat with someone else at lunch. Ana feels a heavy, left-out feeling. Carlos worked on a model bridge for two hours and it finally held a book. He feels warm and tall inside.
look.prompt: Pick a feeling word for Ana and one for Carlos. How would saying the word out loud help each of them?

check.q: What did Theo do that helped?
check.why: Theo said, "I feel embarrassed," which named his feeling.

check.q: What is a feelings vocabulary?
choices: The words you know for naming feelings
check.why: A feelings vocabulary is the set of words you use to name feelings.

check.q: What does frustrated mean?
choices: Upset because something is hard or not going your way
check.why: Frustrated means upset because something is hard or not going the way you want.

lessons.title: What Stress Feels Like
lessons.mainIdea: Stress is the body's way of getting ready for a challenge, and a little is normal.
reading: Imagine it is the morning of the school play. Your stomach flutters. Your mouth feels dry. You keep going over your lines. This is *stress*. Stress is how your body and mind react to a challenge.

When you feel stress, your body makes chemicals called *hormones*. One is adrenaline. It makes your heart beat faster and your breathing speed up. Long ago, this helped people run from danger. Today it can help you focus for a play or a race.

A little stress can help you do your best. Too much stress for too long can make you feel tired, grumpy or sick to your stomach. It can make it hard to sleep. The good news is that there are many ways to help your body calm down.

words.d: how your body and mind react to a challenge or a worry
chemicals your body makes that carry messages through your blood
a hormone that makes your heart beat faster when you feel stress or excitement

look.title: Body Clues
look.text: Before a big test, Sofia notices her shoulders are up near her ears. Her hands are cold. She keeps tapping her pencil. She has not eaten much breakfast.
look.prompt: Which of these clues show that Sofia's body is feeling stress? What might help her?

check.q: What is stress?
choices: How your body and mind react to a challenge
A sickness you catch from others
check.why: The reading defines stress as how your body and mind react to a challenge.

check.q: What does adrenaline do?
check.why: Adrenaline is a hormone that speeds up your heart and breathing.

check.q: What can too much stress for too long do?
choices: Make it hard to sleep and make you feel tired
check.why: The reading says too much stress can make you tired, grumpy and unable to sleep well.

lessons.title: Breathing and Moving
lessons.mainIdea: Slow breathing and moving your body are two simple tools that help calm stress.
reading: Ms. Bell taught Maya to breathe in slowly while counting to four. Then she breathed out slowly while counting to six. After a few breaths, Maya's shoulders dropped. Her tight stomach eased a little.

Slow breathing sends a message to your body that you are safe. Your heart can slow down. This is sometimes called *belly breathing*, because your belly rises as you breathe in. You can do it anywhere, even at your desk.

Moving your body also helps. Running, dancing, biking or walking the dog can burn off stress. Health experts say exercise can improve mood. Many people find that moving outside helps even more. Even a short walk can help you feel calmer.

words.d: slow, deep breathing where your belly rises as you breathe in
moving your body in ways that make your heart and muscles work

look.title: Try It: Four In, Six Out
look.text: Sit up tall. Put one hand on your belly. Breathe in through your nose while you count slowly to four. Feel your hand rise. Breathe out through your mouth while you count to six. Feel your hand fall. Do this three times.
look.prompt: Try it. What did you notice in your body afterward? When could you use this?

check.q: How did Ms. Bell tell Maya to breathe?
choices: In for four, out for six
Holding her breath for a minute
Only through her mouth, very quickly
check.why: Ms. Bell taught Maya to breathe in for four counts and out for six.

check.q: Why is it called belly breathing?
choices: Your belly rises as you breathe in
You breathe through your belly button
You must lie on your belly
check.why: In belly breathing, your belly rises as you take a slow, deep breath.

check.q: Which of these is an example of moving to calm stress?
check.why: The reading says a walk, dancing or biking can help burn off stress.

lessons.title: Talking and Sleeping
lessons.mainIdea: Talking to someone you trust and getting enough sleep both help your mind handle stress.
reading: Maya felt better after she told Ms. Bell her worry. That is common. Sharing a problem with a *trusted adult* can make it feel smaller. A trusted adult is a grown-up who keeps you safe and listens, like a parent, teacher or coach.
Sleep matters too. While you sleep, your brain sorts out the day. It stores what you learned. It also helps you handle feelings. When you are tired, small problems can feel huge.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine says children ages 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Going to bed at the same time each night helps. A quiet, dark room helps too. A calm *bedtime routine*, like reading a book, tells your body it is time to rest.

words.d: a grown-up who keeps you safe and listens, like a parent, teacher, coach or nurse
the same calm steps you do each night before sleep

look.title: How Much Sleep Do People Need?
look.unit: hours a night (middle of the advised range; adults: the least advised)
look.cite: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, Paruthi and others, 2016 (children and teens); Watson and others, 2015 (adults)
look.prompt: Which group needs the most sleep? How does the amount change as people get older?

check.q: What is a trusted adult?
choices: A grown-up who keeps you safe and listens
check.why: A trusted adult is a grown-up like a parent, teacher or coach who listens and keeps you safe.

check.q: About how much sleep do children ages 6 to 12 need?
check.why: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine says 9 to 12 hours for ages 6 to 12.

check.q: What does the brain do while you sleep?
choices: It sorts the day and stores what you learned
check.why: The reading says the brain sorts out the day and stores learning during sleep.

lessons.title: Worry and Sadness Are Common
lessons.mainIdea: Many kids feel worried or sad, and help is available when those feelings stay a long time.
reading: Everyone feels worried sometimes. Everyone feels sad sometimes. A pet dies. A friend moves away. A test is coming. These feelings are a normal part of life. They usually pass after a while.

Sometimes a worry or sadness stays for weeks. It may get in the way of school, play or sleep. When worry is strong and lasts a long time, doctors may call it *anxiety*. When sadness is deep and lasts a long time, doctors may call it *depression*.

These are real health conditions, like asthma is. They are nobody's fault. The CDC reports that anxiety and depression are among the most common mental health conditions in children. Many kids get better with help, such as talking with a counselor. Telling a trusted adult is the first step.

words.d: strong worry or fear that stays a long time and gets in the way of daily life
deep sadness or loss of interest that lasts a long time and needs care

look.title: Passing Cloud or Long Storm?
look.text: Kai felt sad for two days after his team lost. Then he was back to laughing with friends. Rosa has felt sad for more than a month. She stopped drawing, which she used to love, and she does not want to eat much.
look.prompt: How are Kai's and Rosa's feelings different? What would you want Rosa to do?

check.q: What does the reading say about worry and sadness?
choices: They are a normal part of life
They mean you did something wrong
check.why: The reading says everyone feels worried and sad sometimes, and that is normal.

check.q: When might a doctor call strong worry anxiety?
choices: When it happens before a fun party
When it is strong and lasts a long time
check.why: Anxiety is strong worry that lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life.

check.q: What is the first step if sadness stays a long time?
choices: Wait for it to go away alone
check.why: The reading says telling a trusted adult is the first step.

lessons.title: People Who Help
lessons.mainIdea: Counselors, psychologists and doctors are trained to help with feelings and mental health.
reading: Many schools have a *school counselor*, like Ms. Bell. A counselor helps students with feelings, friendships and school problems. You can ask your teacher to visit the counselor. Some schools also have a school social worker who helps students and families.

A *psychologist* is someone who has studied the mind for many years. Psychologists talk with people and teach them skills to handle worry, sadness or anger. Some work in schools. Others work in clinics or hospitals.

Doctors help too. A family doctor or pediatrician checks both body and mind at a checkup. A *psychiatrist* is a medical doctor who focuses on mental health. Asking for help is a strong and smart choice, just like seeing a doctor for a broken arm.

words.d: a trained helper at school who supports students with feelings, friends and school problems
a person trained to study the mind and help people with thoughts and feelings
a medical doctor who focuses on mental health

look.title: Who Could Help?
look.text: Devon has trouble falling asleep because he worries about his parents arguing. Priya feels left out at recess every day. Ben's worry about germs keeps getting bigger. His mom wants to talk with a doctor about it.
look.prompt: For each kid, name one helper from the lesson who could help. Why did you choose that helper?

check.q: What does a school counselor do?
choices: Helps students with feelings, friends and school problems
check.why: A school counselor supports students with feelings, friendships and school problems.

check.q: How is a psychiatrist different from a psychologist?
choices: A psychiatrist only works with animals
A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who focuses on mental health
There is no difference at all
check.why: The reading says a psychiatrist is a medical doctor who focuses on mental health.

check.q: What does the reading say about asking for help?
choices: It is a sign of weakness
It is a strong and smart choice
check.why: The reading compares asking for help to seeing a doctor for a broken arm: a strong, smart choice.

lessons.title: Different Minds
lessons.mainIdea: People's brains learn and feel in different ways, and each mind has strengths.
reading: In Mr. Ortiz's class, Leo remembers every fact about trains. Zara draws amazing comics. Sam learns best by moving around. Nia needs quiet to focus. Each brain works in its own way.

Scientists use the word *neurodiversity* to describe how brains naturally differ. Some people are autistic. Some have ADHD, which can affect focus and energy. Some have dyslexia, which affects how the brain handles written words. These are different ways of learning and feeling.

What helps is finding the right tools. A student with dyslexia might use audiobooks. A student with ADHD might take movement breaks. Headphones can help someone who notices sounds strongly. Tools like these are called *supports*. Every mind has strengths to grow.

words.d: the natural differences in how people's brains learn, think and feel
tools or changes that help a person learn or feel comfortable, like audiobooks or quiet spaces

look.title: The Right Tool
look.text: Omar reads more easily when he listens to the book while following the words. Grace focuses better when she can stand at a tall desk. Eli feels calmer at assemblies when he wears soft headphones.
look.prompt: What support does each student use? Why might one tool help one person but not another?

check.q: What does neurodiversity mean?
choices: Everyone's brain is exactly the same
The natural differences in how brains learn and feel
check.why: Neurodiversity describes the natural ways people's brains differ.

check.q: Which support might help a student with dyslexia?
check.why: The reading says a student with dyslexia might use audiobooks.

check.q: What is dyslexia?
choices: A way the brain handles written words differently
check.why: The reading says dyslexia affects how the brain handles written words.

lessons.title: Kindness and Including Others
lessons.mainIdea: Being kind and including others helps everyone's mental health, including your own.
reading: At recess, a new student named Hana stood alone by the fence. Diego walked over and asked, "Want to play four square?" Hana smiled. By the end of the week, she had three new friends.

Feeling left out can hurt. Feeling *included* helps people feel safe and happy. Including someone means inviting them in, listening and making room. Small acts count, like saving a seat or saying hello.

Kindness helps the helper too. Studies have found that doing kind things can lift your own mood. Putting yourself in someone else's shoes is called *empathy*. When you notice how someone feels and act kindly, you make your whole school a healthier place.

words.d: invited in and made to feel part of a group
understanding and caring about how someone else feels

look.title: Room at the Table
look.text: At lunch, a table has five friends and one empty chair. A student from another class walks by holding a tray and looks around the busy room.
look.prompt: What could one friend at the table do or say? How might everyone feel afterward?

check.q: What did Diego do for Hana?
check.why: Diego asked Hana to play four square, which included her.

check.q: What is empathy?
choices: Being the best at a game
Understanding and caring about how someone else feels
check.why: Empathy is understanding and caring about someone else's feelings.

check.q: How can kindness help the helper?
choices: It can lift the helper's own mood
It gets the helper out of homework
It has no effect on the helper
check.why: The reading says studies found kind acts can lift your own mood.

lessons.title: Screens and Sleep
lessons.mainIdea: Putting screens away before bed helps your brain rest and your mood stay steady.
reading: It is 9:30 at night. Jordan is in bed playing a game on a tablet. One more level, he thinks. Then one more. At 10:45 he finally puts it down. The next morning he is tired and cranky.

Screens like phones, tablets and TVs give off bright light. Some of this is *blue light*. Bright light at night can tell your brain it is still daytime. Your body makes a sleep hormone called *melatonin* when it gets dark. Bright screens can delay it.

Games and videos also keep your brain busy and excited. The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests keeping screens out of the bedroom at night. It also suggests turning them off 30 to 60 minutes before bed. A book, a bath or quiet music can help you wind down instead.

words.d: a kind of bright light given off by screens and the sun
a hormone your body makes in the dark that helps you feel sleepy
the time spent looking at phones, tablets, computers or TV

look.title: Two Evenings
look.text: Evening A: Mia watches videos in bed until 10:30 with the lights off. Evening B: Mia turns off her tablet at 8:30, takes a shower, and reads a paper book until she feels sleepy at 9:00.
look.prompt: On which evening will Mia probably sleep better? Use the words melatonin and blue light in your answer.

check.q: What does melatonin do?
check.why: Melatonin is a hormone made in the dark that helps you feel sleepy.

check.q: How can bright screens at night affect sleep?
choices: They can tell your brain it is still daytime
check.why: The reading says bright light at night can trick the brain into thinking it is day and delay melatonin.

check.q: What does the American Academy of Pediatrics suggest?
choices: Play games until you fall asleep
Turn screens off 30 to 60 minutes before bed
check.why: The AAP suggests turning screens off 30 to 60 minutes before bed and keeping them out of the bedroom at night.

lessons.title: Your Calm-Down Plan
lessons.mainIdea: A calm-down plan lists the tools that help you, so you can use them when feelings get big.
reading: After her talk with Ms. Bell, Maya made a card. On it she wrote: breathe four in, six out. Squeeze a smooth stone. Draw. Talk to Mom or Ms. Bell. She kept the card in her backpack.
Maya made a *calm-down plan*. It is a short list of things that help you when feelings get big. Having it written down helps, because strong feelings can make it hard to think of ideas.

Every plan is different. Some people like music. Some like to stretch or hug a pet. Some need a quiet corner. The best plan always includes at least one trusted adult to talk to. Practicing your tools on calm days makes them easier to use on hard days. This is called *coping*.

words.d: a short written list of things that help you when feelings get big
using healthy ways to handle hard feelings or problems

look.title: Build Your Card
look.text: Picture an index card. At the top it says: When my feelings get big, I can... Below are four empty lines. The last line says: A grown-up I can talk to is...
look.prompt: What four things would you write on your card? Who is your trusted adult?

check.q: What is a calm-down plan?
choices: A short list of things that help when feelings get big
check.why: A calm-down plan lists tools that help you when feelings get big.

check.q: Why does writing the plan down help?
choices: Strong feelings can make it hard to think of ideas
check.why: The reading says strong feelings can make it hard to think, so a written plan helps.

check.q: What should every calm-down plan include?
choices: At least one trusted adult to talk to
check.why: The reading says the best plan always includes a trusted adult.

review.q: What does Maya's story show about sharing a worry?
choices: It can make the worry feel lighter
review.why: Maya's worry felt lighter after she told the school counselor.

review.q: Which part of the body makes feelings?
review.why: The brain is the control center that makes emotions.

review.q: Which is a healthy way to calm stress?
review.why: Slow belly breathing tells the body it is safe and helps it calm down.

review.q: Which hormone speeds up your heart when you feel stress?
review.why: Adrenaline makes your heart and breathing speed up.

review.q: Who is a medical doctor who focuses on mental health?
review.why: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who focuses on mental health.

choices: The natural differences in how brains work
review.why: Neurodiversity means brains naturally learn and feel in different ways.

review.q: Why can screens at bedtime make it harder to sleep?
choices: Their bright light can delay melatonin
They make the room too cold
review.why: Bright light at night can trick the brain and delay the sleep hormone melatonin.

choices: Understanding and caring about how someone else feels
review.why: Empathy means understanding and caring about someone else's feelings.
